transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, yeah, thanks for seeing me. So, what brings me in... well, I'm a supervisor for a sales team—not retail, it's outside sales—and a big part of my job is keeping track of everyone's metrics, making sure the procedures are followed, that kind of thing. But I just keep making these really dumb mistakes on our sales reports. 

Like, we have this team dashboard, right? It updates all the time, and at the end of the week, I have to pull the numbers to send up the chain to the regional manager. It should be straightforward. But I'll end up copying the exact wrong numbers from the dashboard. I'll put my top guy's numbers in the wrong column, or I'll completely scramble the totals. And it's not just the numbers, it's the daily procedures, too. There's a compliance checklist I have to go through for my team's accounts, and I'll just completely miss a line I was supposed to check. 

The most frustrating part, and I guess why I finally made the appointment, is that I *know* I need to be careful. So I sit there, and I swear to you, I go over it. I look right at the screen, I think I've checked everything perfectly, I tell myself it's good to go, and then my boss calls me on Monday asking why the weekly estimates make zero sense. It's just embarrassing, you know? I'm a 36-year-old supervisor, I shouldn't be making these rookie mistakes, but no matter how hard I stare at the spreadsheet, my brain just... skips over things. You can only say "my bad" so many times before people start looking at you funny, so I just really need to figure out why I keep doing this.
Outside of work, do you find yourself making similar kinds of mistakes—like missing details, losing things, or not being able to stay focused on tasks at home or in other situations?

Oh, man, losing things... yeah. It's everywhere. You asked about outside of work, and yes, at home I'm constantly—and I mean constantly—doing this little pocket pat-down dance. But it really follows me everywhere, which just adds to that whole embarrassment factor I was telling you about with my job. 

I mean, I am just always hunting for my phone, or my keys, or my work badge. The badge is a huge one. I've tried putting it on a lanyard, I've tried one of those retractable belt clips, but I'll take it off because it's annoying me while I'm driving, set it on the passenger seat, and then the next morning I'm tearing my house and my car apart looking for it. 

And it's not even just small things like keys. I will literally have a folder in my hand—like, the physical printed-out route sheets for the day—I'll set it down for half a second to grab my coffee mug, turn back around, and it's just gone. I have no idea where I put it. It gets so incredibly embarrassing, especially when my reps are all standing around the whiteboard waiting on me to start the morning meeting. They're all looking at me, ready to get their assignments and hit the road, and I'm frantically digging through my briefcase or speed-walking back to my desk to find the folder I literally just had in my hand two seconds ago. You can see them kind of exchanging looks, like, aren't you supposed to be the guy in charge? I always try to laugh it off and say something stupid like, "Oh, rough morning, guys," but inside I'm just kicking myself because it happens all the time. I just put things down and they completely cease to exist in my brain.
When you think about times before adulthood—like when you were in school or doing chores at home—did you have similar problems with losing things, missing details, or struggling to stay focused?

Oh, yeah. Yeah, absolutely. I mean, it’s not like this just started happening when I got promoted, you know? It’s been this way for as long as I can remember. If you ask my mom, she’ll probably talk your ear off about it. She actually still brings it up sometimes, especially around the holidays when she’s telling embarrassing stories about me to my wife. 

She kept all these old report cards and notes from my teachers, going all the way back to, like, second or third grade. And it’s always the same stuff. The teachers would write these long paragraphs—I actually saw one recently when we were cleaning out her attic—and they’d say things like, "He rushes through his assignments," or "He makes careless errors," which sounds exactly like what I’m doing with the sales reports now, right? And the homework... man, the homework. I would do it, I swear I would do it sitting at the kitchen table, and then the next day the teacher would ask for it, and it was just... gone. Not in my backpack, not in my desk. Just vanished. My mom said she used to get calls about me losing my assignments at least once a week.

And it wasn't just losing things or making mistakes, either. The notes always talked about how I couldn't just sit still and do the work. They’d say I was always talking out of turn, interrupting other kids, or just blurting things out before the teacher even finished asking the question. And staying in my seat? Forget about it. The teachers were constantly having to remind me to sit down. I’d be up sharpening my pencil for the fifth time, or walking over to look out the window, or just standing by my desk for no reason. It’s funny, looking back, because I still kind of do that—like when I’m at my desk at work, I’m always shifting around or getting up to grab water when I should be focusing on the dashboard. But yeah, as a kid, it was definitely a huge issue. The teachers were always telling my parents I needed to pay better attention and stop rushing, but I just... I don't know, I just couldn't seem to slow my brain down enough to do it the way they wanted me to. So, yeah, this is definitely not a new problem for me.
